A nut is dry, and the whole pericarp is hard or stony. An acorn is a nut. A pome is fleshy because the receptacle enlarges. An apple is a pome.

options: A fleshy fruit from an inferior compound ovary with many seeds. The enlarged receptacle is the fleshy accessory tissue. An apple is a pome.
A fleshy fruit from a compound superior ovary with many seeds. The seeds are embedded in the flesh. A tomato is one.
A fruit with one seed, a hard endocarp, a fleshy mesocarp, and a thin exocarp. A cherry is one.
A dry fruit from compound ovaries. It splits open along the top. An iris fruit is one.
questions.answer: A fleshy fruit from an inferior compound ovary with many seeds. The enlarged receptacle is the fleshy accessory tissue. An apple is a pome.
questions.explanation: A pome is derived from a flower with an inferior compound ovary and many seeds. An inferior ovary sits below the attachment of the other flower parts. The receptacle enlarges and becomes the fleshy part of this accessory fruit. An apple is a pome. Accessory tissue is fruit tissue that did not come from the ovary. A berry comes from a superior ovary, and the flesh is the mesocarp. A tomato is a berry. A drupe has one seed and a hard endocarp. A cherry is a drupe. A capsule is dry and splits open. An iris fruit is a capsule.

options: It forms from one ovary. That ovary may be simple or compound.
It is composed of more than one ovary.
It forms from many separate ovaries of a single flower.
It forms from the ovaries of several flowers that have grown together.
questions.answer: It forms from one ovary. That ovary may be simple or compound.
questions.explanation: A simple fruit forms from one ovary. That ovary may be a simple ovary, from one carpel, or a compound ovary, from more than one carpel. A tomato is a simple fruit: it comes from one compound ovary. An iris capsule is also a simple fruit. A simple fruit may be fleshy, like a tomato, or dry, like a capsule. A compound fruit is composed of more than one ovary. An aggregate fruit, such as a blackberry, comes from many separate ovaries of one flower. A multiple fruit, such as a pineapple, comes from the ovaries of several flowers that have grown together.

options: Animals disperse it. The seeds have a hard seed coat that breaks during digestion.
It may split open at maturity or remain closed.
It is composed of more than one ovary.
A significant portion of the edible flesh develops from tissue outside the ovaries.
questions.answer: Animals disperse it. The seeds have a hard seed coat that breaks during digestion.
questions.explanation: A fleshy fruit is dispersed by animals. Its seeds have a hard seed coat that breaks during digestion. A tomato, a cherry, and an apple are fleshy fruits. A dry fruit may split open at maturity, which is dehiscent, or remain closed, which is indehiscent. A capsule splits open. A grain remains closed. A compound fruit is composed of more than one ovary. An accessory fruit has a significant portion of its edible flesh from tissue outside the ovaries. An apple is both fleshy and accessory. Accessory names the source of the flesh. Fleshy names the animal-dispersed fruit with that hard seed coat.

options: It may split open at maturity, which is dehiscent, or remain closed, which is indehiscent.
Animals disperse it. The seeds have a hard seed coat that breaks during digestion.
It forms from many separate ovaries of a single flower.
It forms from the ovaries of several flowers that have grown together.
questions.answer: It may split open at maturity, which is dehiscent, or remain closed, which is indehiscent.
questions.explanation: A dry fruit may be dehiscent or indehiscent. Dehiscent means it splits open at maturity. A capsule, a legume, and a follicle are dehiscent. Indehiscent means it remains closed. An achene, a samara, a grain, and a nut are indehiscent. A fleshy fruit is dispersed by animals, and the seed coat breaks during digestion. An aggregate fruit, such as a blackberry, forms from many separate ovaries of one flower. A multiple fruit, such as a pineapple, forms from several flowers grown together.

options: It is composed of more than one ovary.
It forms from one ovary, and that ovary may be compound.
Animals disperse it. The seeds have a hard seed coat that breaks during digestion.
It may split open at maturity or remain closed.
questions.answer: It is composed of more than one ovary.
questions.explanation: A compound fruit is composed of more than one ovary. It falls into two categories. An aggregate fruit is derived from many separate ovaries of a single flower. A blackberry is an aggregate fruit. A multiple fruit is derived from the enlarged ovaries of multiple flowers that have grown together. A pineapple is a multiple fruit. A simple fruit forms from one ovary, even when that ovary is compound. A tomato and an iris capsule are simple fruits. A fleshy fruit is the animal-dispersed type. A dry fruit splits open or remains closed.

options: It is derived from many separate ovaries of a single flower. A blackberry is an aggregate fruit.
It is derived from the enlarged ovaries of multiple flowers that have grown together. A pineapple is one.
It forms from one ovary. That ovary may be simple or compound.
A significant portion of the edible flesh develops from tissue outside the ovaries. An apple is one.
questions.answer: It is derived from many separate ovaries of a single flower. A blackberry is an aggregate fruit.
questions.explanation: An aggregate fruit is a compound fruit derived from many separate ovaries of a single flower. A blackberry is an aggregate fruit. A multiple fruit comes from the enlarged ovaries of multiple flowers that have grown together. A pineapple is a multiple fruit. A simple fruit forms from one ovary. A tomato is a simple fruit. An accessory fruit gets a significant portion of its edible flesh from tissue outside the ovaries. An apple is an accessory fruit.

options: It is derived from the enlarged ovaries of multiple flowers that have grown together. A pineapple is a multiple fruit.
It is derived from many separate ovaries of a single flower. A blackberry is one.
It forms from one ovary. That ovary may be simple or compound.
A significant portion of the edible flesh develops from tissue outside the ovaries. An apple is one.
questions.answer: It is derived from the enlarged ovaries of multiple flowers that have grown together. A pineapple is a multiple fruit.
questions.explanation: A multiple fruit is a compound fruit derived from the enlarged ovaries of multiple flowers that have grown together. A pineapple is a multiple fruit. An aggregate fruit comes from many separate ovaries of one flower. A blackberry is an aggregate fruit. A simple fruit forms from one ovary. A tomato is a simple fruit. An accessory fruit gets a significant portion of its edible flesh from tissue outside the ovaries. An apple is an accessory fruit.

options: A significant portion of the edible flesh develops from plant tissues outside the ovaries. An apple is an accessory fruit.
It is derived from many separate ovaries of a single flower. A blackberry is one.
It is derived from the enlarged ovaries of multiple flowers that have grown together. A pineapple is one.
It forms from one compound ovary, and the seeds are embedded in the ovary wall. A tomato is one.
questions.answer: A significant portion of the edible flesh develops from plant tissues outside the ovaries. An apple is an accessory fruit.
questions.explanation: An accessory fruit gets a significant portion of its edible flesh from plant tissues outside the ovaries. In an apple, that tissue is the enlarged receptacle. An apple is also a pome. A blackberry is an aggregate fruit, from many separate ovaries of one flower. A pineapple is a multiple fruit, from the ovaries of several flowers grown together. A tomato forms from one compound ovary, and the seeds are embedded in the fleshy mesocarp of that ovary. A tomato is a berry, and it is a simple fruit.

prompt.text: In a flower, what is pollination?

options: The transfer of a pollen grain, the male gametophyte, to the stigma.
One sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote. The other sperm joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm.
The pollen tube grows down the style toward an ovule.
A mature seed is carried away from the parent plant.
questions.answer: The transfer of a pollen grain, the male gametophyte, to the stigma.
questions.explanation: In a flower, pollination is the transfer of a pollen grain to the stigma. The pollen grain is the male gametophyte. After it lands, a pollen tube grows down the style toward an ovule. Growth of that tube is not pollination, and it is not fertilization. Fertilization is the fusion that follows: one sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote, and the other sperm joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm. Carrying a mature seed away from the parent is seed dispersal. In conifers and other gymnosperms, pollen is delivered to the ovule itself, because those plants have no stigma.

prompt.text: In a flower, what is fertilization?

options: One sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote. The other sperm joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm.
A pollen grain, the male gametophyte, is transferred to the stigma.
The pollen tube grows down the style toward an ovule.
A mature seed is carried away from the parent plant.
questions.answer: One sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote. The other sperm joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm.
questions.explanation: In a flower, fertilization is the fusion of the sperm with the cells of the embryo sac. One sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote. The zygote develops into the embryo. The other sperm joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm, the seed's supply of stored food. This pair of fusions is double fertilization. Pollination happens earlier: a pollen grain, the male gametophyte, is transferred to the stigma. The pollen tube then grows down the style and carries the sperm to the ovule. Growth of the tube is not itself fertilization. Carrying a mature seed away from the parent is seed dispersal.

options: A mature ovary. It encloses the seeds and helps disperse them.
A fertilized ovule. It contains the embryo and the stored food.
A seed exposed on a cone scale.
The receptacle of every flower, whether or not an ovary is present.
questions.answer: A mature ovary. It encloses the seeds and helps disperse them.
questions.explanation: A fruit is a mature ovary of a flowering plant. The ovary wall becomes the pericarp, and the fruit encloses the seeds and helps disperse them. A seed is a fertilized ovule, and it is what the fruit contains. A pine seed sits exposed on a cone scale. A pine does not make a fruit. The receptacle becomes the fleshy part of an accessory fruit such as an apple, but the fruit still develops in connection with the ovary. A receptacle without a matured ovary is not a fruit.

prompt.text: How did the sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels of a flower evolve?

options: They evolved as modified leaves.
They evolved as modified roots.
They evolved as four separate kinds of stems.
They evolved from the cone scales of a pine.
questions.answer: They evolved as modified leaves.
questions.explanation: The four organs of a flower evolved as modified leaves. Sepals enclose and protect the bud. Petals attract pollinators. Stamens are the male part and produce pollen. The carpel, also called the pistil, is the female part and receives pollen. The ABC hypothesis says which of those leaf-derived organs develops where. Roots absorb water. A stem is the axis that bears the leaves. Pine cone scales are gymnosperm structures. They are not the four organs of a flower.

prompt.text: Which living plant is the sister group to all other living flowering plants?

options: Amborella.
A water lily.
A magnoliid, such as a magnolia.
A monocot, such as a grass.
questions.answer: Amborella.
questions.explanation: In the usual flowering-plant tree, Amborella is the sister group to all other living angiosperms. Water lilies, star anise and its relatives, and magnoliids branch off after Amborella. Monocots and eudicots are the two clades that include most living flowering plants. A grass is a monocot. It is not the sister group to every other flowering plant.

prompt.text: Which two groups include most living flowering plants?

options: Monocots and eudicots.
Amborella and the water lilies.
Magnoliids and star anise.
Conifers and cycads.
questions.answer: Monocots and eudicots.
questions.explanation: Monocots and eudicots include most living flowering plants. A monocot embryo has one cotyledon. An eudicot embryo has two. Amborella, water lilies, star anise and its relatives, and magnoliids are smaller branches that split off before those two large clades. Conifers and cycads are gymnosperms. They do not make flowers.

prompt.text: A flower is small and green. It has no nectar, and it releases a large amount of pollen. How is it most likely pollinated?

options: By the wind.
By an animal seeking nectar.
By a bee that must land on a broad petal.
By water that carries a single heavy pollen grain.
questions.answer: By the wind.
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers are often small and green, without nectar or showy petals, and they release a large amount of pollen. Grasses are a common example. An animal-pollinated flower usually offers a reward, such as nectar, and has petals that attract the visitor. A bee landing on a broad petal is animal pollination. Water pollination is uncommon, and those grains are not the dry, abundant pollen of a wind-pollinated flower.

prompt.text: A flower has bright petals and nectaries that offer a nectar reward. How is it most likely pollinated?

options: By an animal.
By the wind.
By releasing spores from a sporangium.
By the seed falling from a cone scale.
questions.answer: By an animal.
questions.explanation: Bright petals and nectar rewards attract an animal, which carries pollen from one flower to another. Petals are the corolla, and their role is to attract pollinators. Wind-pollinated flowers usually lack nectar and showy petals. Releasing spores is the seedless-plant pattern. A seed falling from a cone scale is gymnosperm seed dispersal, not pollination of a flower.

prompt.text: A plant's pollen cannot fertilize the carpels of that same plant. What strategy is this?

options: Self-incompatibility.
The stamens and the carpels mature at different times.
Wind pollination of a flower with no petals.
Dispersal of the fruit by an animal.
questions.answer: Self-incompatibility.
questions.explanation: Self-incompatibility means a plant's own pollen cannot fertilize its own carpels, so the offspring are not produced by self-pollination. Maturation of stamens and carpels at different times is a different strategy. The pollen is released when the stigma of that flower cannot receive it, or the stigma is ready before the pollen. Wind pollination is a way to move pollen. It does not by itself stop self-pollination. Fruit dispersal moves seeds. It happens after fertilization. A dioecious species also avoids self-pollination, because the staminate and pistillate flowers are on separate plants.

prompt.text: A flower releases its pollen several days before its stigma can receive pollen. What strategy is this?

options: The stamens and the carpels mature at different times.
Self-incompatibility. The pollen cannot fertilize that plant's own carpels.
The flower is pollinated by the wind.
The plant produces seeds without fertilization.
questions.answer: The stamens and the carpels mature at different times.
questions.explanation: If the stamens and the carpels mature at different times, the flower's own pollen is not available when its stigma can receive pollen. That reduces self-pollination. Self-incompatibility is a different strategy: the pollen lands, but it cannot fertilize that same plant. Wind pollination is a means of moving pollen, not a timing strategy. Seeds produced without fertilization are apomixis, a form of asexual reproduction.

prompt.text: In a mature bean seed, an eudicot, where is most of the stored food?

options: In the two cotyledons. The endosperm was absorbed as the seed developed.
In the endosperm. The cotyledons absorb it only after germination begins.
In the seed coat.
In tissue of the female gametophyte, as in a pine.
questions.answer: In the two cotyledons. The endosperm was absorbed as the seed developed.
questions.explanation: A bean is an eudicot, so the embryo has two cotyledons. As the seed develops, those cotyledons absorb the endosperm, and the mature seed stores most of its food there. A corn grain is a monocot. Its endosperm remains, and the single cotyledon absorbs that food during germination. The seed coat is the protective layer, not the food. Female-gametophyte tissue is the stored food of a pine, which does not make endosperm.

prompt.text: In a mature corn grain, a monocot, where is most of the stored food?

options: In the endosperm. The single cotyledon absorbs it during germination.
In two cotyledons. The endosperm was absorbed before the seed matured.
In the seed coat.
In tissue of the female gametophyte.
questions.answer: In the endosperm. The single cotyledon absorbs it during germination.
questions.explanation: A corn grain is a monocot fruit with one seed. The embryo has one cotyledon. Most of the stored food remains in the endosperm, and that cotyledon absorbs it during germination. Gibberellins from the grass embryo also trigger starch breakdown in the endosperm. A bean stores the food in two cotyledons after the endosperm has been absorbed. The seed coat is not the food. Female-gametophyte tissue is the food supply of a pine.

prompt.text: As a bean seedling emerges, what pulls the cotyledons above the soil?

options: A hook in the hypocotyl, the embryonic stem below the cotyledons.
A coleoptile, a sheath around the young shoot.
The endosperm, which pushes the seed coat upward.
The radicle, which is the embryonic root.
questions.answer: A hook in the hypocotyl, the embryonic stem below the cotyledons.
questions.explanation: In a bean, the hypocotyl forms a hook that pulls the cotyledons above the soil. The hook then straightens. A coleoptile is the sheath that protects a corn shoot as it grows up through the soil. Corn does not pull two cotyledons above ground. The endosperm is stored food. It does not push the seed coat up. The radicle is the embryonic root. It emerges first and grows down.

prompt.text: As a corn seedling emerges, what protects the young shoot?

options: A coleoptile, a sheath around the shoot.
A hook in the hypocotyl that pulls two cotyledons above the soil.
The seed coat, which grows up with the shoot.
The endosperm, which surrounds the leaves after they emerge.
questions.answer: A coleoptile, a sheath around the shoot.
questions.explanation: A corn shoot is protected by a coleoptile, a sheath, as it pushes through the soil. The leaves then break out of that sheath. A bean uses a hypocotyl hook to pull its two cotyledons above the soil. Corn has one cotyledon, and it stays with the endosperm in the grain. The seed coat does not grow up with the shoot. The endosperm is the stored food left in the grain. It does not surround the emerged leaves.

prompt.text: A strawberry plant grows a runner, and a new plant forms at the tip. What kind of reproduction is this?

options: Asexual reproduction. The new plant grows from the parent without fertilization.
Sexual reproduction. The runner is a fruit that carries a fertilized seed.
Pollination. The runner transfers pollen to a stigma.
Apomixis. The runner is a seed produced without fertilization.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction. The new plant grows from the parent without fertilization.
questions.explanation: A runner is a form of asexual, or vegetative, reproduction. The new plant grows from the body of the parent, with no fertilization, so it is genetically the same as that parent apart from mutation. A fruit carries seeds produced after fertilization. Pollination moves a pollen grain. Apomixis is asexual production of a seed, without fertilization. A runner is not a seed.

options: Production of seeds without fertilization.
Production of a new plant from a runner or a tuber.
Transfer of pollen from one plant to the stigma of another.
Fusion of one sperm with the egg and one sperm with the polar nuclei.
questions.answer: Production of seeds without fertilization.
questions.explanation: Apomixis is the production of seeds without fertilization. The embryo develops without the fusion of sperm and egg, so the reproduction is asexual. A runner or a tuber also produces a new plant without fertilization, but that new plant does not come from a seed. Transfer of pollen is pollination. Fusion of a sperm with the egg and a sperm with the polar nuclei is double fertilization, which is sexual.

prompt.text: Select every way people depend on plants.

bank: Food, including grains, fruits, and vegetables
Wood, paper, and plant fibers such as cotton
The nitrogen gas that makes up most of the atmosphere
answers: Food, including grains, fruits, and vegetables
Wood, paper, and plant fibers such as cotton
questions.explanation: People depend on plants for food, for oxygen released during photosynthesis, for wood, paper, and fibers such as cotton, and for medicines first identified in plants. Dietary vitamin B12 is produced by bacteria, not by plants. The nitrogen gas that makes up most of the atmosphere is not a product plants supply to people. Some plants host bacteria that fix nitrogen into a form the plant can use. That is not the same as producing the nitrogen gas in the air.

options: People choose which individuals breed, and the population changes over generations.
A plant inserts a new gene into its own wild relatives by wind pollination.
Natural differences in survival change a population, with no human choice of parents.
A farmer plants a refuge of unmodified crop beside a modified crop.
questions.answer: People choose which individuals breed, and the population changes over generations.
questions.explanation: Artificial selection means people choose which individuals breed. Over generations the crop changes in the direction of the chosen traits. A new gene moving into wild relatives is gene flow. It is a concern with genetically modified crops, not the definition of artificial selection. Change caused by differences in survival, with no person choosing the parents, is natural selection. A refuge of unmodified crop is a way to slow pest resistance to a Bt crop.

prompt.text: How has artificial selection been used on crop plants?

options: People have bred crops for traits such as larger, more edible seeds. Maize was bred from teosinte.
People have waited for natural selection to change wild plants, without choosing parents.
People have moved one gene from a bacterium into a crop by genetic engineering.
People have stopped all reproduction so the crop stays identical to its wild ancestor.
questions.answer: People have bred crops for traits such as larger, more edible seeds. Maize was bred from teosinte.
questions.explanation: Artificial selection has been used extensively on crops. People saved seed from plants with traits they wanted, such as larger grains or fruits that are easier to eat. Maize was bred from teosinte by that repeated choice. Natural selection does not depend on a person choosing the parents. Moving a bacterial gene into a crop is genetic engineering, a later and more direct method. Stopping reproduction would not produce maize from teosinte.

prompt.text: What is one benefit of a genetically modified crop such as a Bt crop?

options: The plant makes a protein that kills certain insect pests, so the harvest is protected.
The plant no longer needs sunlight or water.
The new gene cannot move to any other plant.
Pests cannot evolve resistance to the new protein.
questions.answer: The plant makes a protein that kills certain insect pests, so the harvest is protected.
questions.explanation: A Bt crop has a gene, originally from a bacterium, for a protein that kills certain insect pests. The benefit is a protected harvest with less dependence on sprayed insecticide. The plant still needs sunlight and water. Pollen or seed can still move a nuclear gene to another plant. Pests can evolve resistance, which is why a refuge of non-Bt plants is planted nearby.

prompt.text: What is one cost of planting a genetically modified crop?

options: A pest can evolve resistance, and the new gene can spread to wild relatives.
The crop can no longer produce seeds of any kind.
Photosynthesis stops because the new gene replaces chlorophyll.
The crop loses its flowers, so it cannot be an angiosperm.
questions.answer: A pest can evolve resistance, and the new gene can spread to wild relatives.
questions.explanation: Two costs are widely discussed. Insect pests can evolve resistance to a Bt protein, so the protection fails. A new gene can also spread to wild relatives by pollen. A modified crop can still make seeds. Photosynthesis continues. The plant remains a flowering plant if it was one. The benefit of a Bt crop is that the plant itself kills certain insect pests.

prompt.text: A Bt crop kills certain insect pests. What practice slows the evolution of resistance in those pests?

options: Plant a refuge of non-Bt crop, so susceptible insects survive and mate with resistant ones.
Spray a broad insecticide over every neighboring species, including insects that do not eat the crop.
Remove all flowers so the crop cannot make pollen.
Plant only Bt seed, with no unmodified plants anywhere nearby.
questions.answer: Plant a refuge of non-Bt crop, so susceptible insects survive and mate with resistant ones.
questions.explanation: A refuge of non-Bt crop lets some susceptible insects survive. They mate with resistant insects, and many of the offspring are still killed by the Bt protein. That slows the spread of resistance. Spraying every neighboring insect harms non-target species. It is not the refuge strategy. Removing all flowers would stop reproduction of the crop. Planting only Bt seed, with no refuge, is the condition under which resistance evolves fastest. A separate way to limit spread of a nuclear gene is to put the gene in the chloroplast, because pollen usually does not carry chloroplast genes.

options: The small opening in the integuments. The pollen tube enters the ovule through it.
A protective layer around the megasporangium. It becomes the seed coat.
The supply of stored food formed when a sperm joins the two polar nuclei.
The mature ovary that encloses the seeds.
questions.answer: The small opening in the integuments. The pollen tube enters the ovule through it.
questions.explanation: A micropyle is the small opening left where the integuments do not completely cover the megasporangium. The pollen tube enters the ovule through that opening. The egg and the two synergids sit at this micropylar end of the embryo sac. An integument is the protective layer around the megasporangium, and it becomes the seed coat. Endosperm is the stored food formed when a sperm joins the two polar nuclei. A fruit is a mature ovary.

options: A protective layer around the megasporangium. It becomes the seed coat.
The small opening where the pollen tube enters the ovule.
The embryo inside a fertilized ovule.
The supply of stored food in a seed.
questions.answer: A protective layer around the megasporangium. It becomes the seed coat.
questions.explanation: An integument is a protective layer of tissue around the megasporangium. After fertilization it becomes the seed coat. The integuments do not close completely. The remaining opening is the micropyle, and the pollen tube enters through it. The embryo is what the fertilized ovule contains. The stored food is a separate part of the seed. In a flowering plant that food is endosperm. A seedless plant such as Selaginella has a megasporangium with no integument around it.
